newsitem.title: USA: World gold demand robust in 4th qtr - WGC analyst.
newsitem.headline: World gold demand robust in 4th qtr - WGC analyst.

text.p: World-wide demand for gold remains strong as the slide in gold prices in recent months continued into the new year, manager of market analysis, George Milling-Stanley, a manager with New York-based World Gold Council, told Reuters Thursday.
"All the evidence to hand indicates that demand remained strong through the fourth quarter, and indeed into the start of the first quarter of 1997," he said.
"Physical demand in 1996 continued to consolidate close to the all-time high recorded in 1995," Milling-Stanley added.
Earlier, World Gold Council reported physical demand in the first nine months of 1996 was running three percent below the 1995 record.

Gold prices have fallen about $13.00 or 3.5 pct since the start of 1997 to a fresh three-year low of $354.50 an ounce Thursday morning in London. They had climbed to a five-year high of $417.00 in February 1996.
"Imports into major distribution centers have been robust in recent months," he said.

Earlier, CRU International reported that imports of bullion into the big six import markets (Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Dubai and Turkey) for the first 10 months of 1996 were down 13 percent on 1995.
But "it is important to remember that increasing liberalization and deregulation of gold markets means more gold is being shipped direct into consumer markets," Milling-Stanley said.

"As a result, it has become necessary to look beyond the statistics on shipments into major distribution centers in order to make a meaningful assessment of the strength of physical demand in key consuming areas," he said.
Nevertheless, Singapore's imports of gold in December, at 28 tonnes, are estimated at 81 percent above the level for December 1995, Milling-Stanley said.

Full year 1996 imports are expected to reach the highest level for four years at 355/360 tonnes, six percent above 1995 and the second highest level ever recorded behind only 1992, when the total was boosted by Indian liberalization, he said.

Hong Kong gold imports in November are estimated at 25 tonnes, up 44 pct on November 1995, and December Hong Kong imports are estimated at 28 tonnes, almost three times the December 1995 level, bringing the fourth quarter 1996 total to 78.2 tonnes, up 84 pct on fourth quarter 1995.
Taiwan gold imports in December are reported to be up 126 pct on December 1995, Milling-Stanley said.
For Dubai, "indications are that record imports in November were maintained during December, with estimates between 30 and 35 tonnes," he said.
"And note that the total for the first 11 months of 1996 surpassed the total for the whole of 1995, which was itself a record year," Milling-Stanley said.

Among the large consuming countries, the best estimate for Indian trade purchases in 1996 is 507 tonnes, six percent above the record of 477 tonnes set in 1995, he said. "The market is already taking advantage of further liberalization by the government, which has doubled the quantities non-resident Indians are allowed to carry out of the country."
In Saudi Arabia, consumer demand in 1996 is estimated at 177 tonnes, with trade purchases expected to match 1995 levels (190 to 195 tonnes) reflecting inventory build-up before the month of Ramadan.
In Turkey, full-year imports reached a six year high at 134.6 tonnes, up 20 pct on 1995.
In the U.S., the dollar value of gold jewelry retail sales in November was up 2.5 pct on November 1995, bringing the year-to-date rise to 5.7 pct.
"Note also that Russia has bought 100 tonnes of gold during the year," Milling-Stanley said.

The gold price has been falling lately, with sentiment undermined by rumors of heavy sales by European central banks in advance of the introduction of European monetary union in 1999, Milling-Stanley said.

"But so far no single central bank has been positively identified, not even by GFMS (Gold Fields Mineral Services), as a seller during the second half of the year, in spite of months of diligent research," he said.

On Tuesday, GFMS reported that official sector sales were the main cause of gold price weakness in late 1996 and said official sector sales amounted to an estimated 123 tonnes in the second half of 1996, bringing the full year total to 208 tonnes.

"The EMI (European Monetary Institute) has made it clear that the Maastricht convergence criteria are designed to demonstrate the health of a country's economy over a period of years and that last minute asset disposals or window dressing will not allow countries to qualify for EMU," he said. "This view has been supported by the Bank of England, Banque de France and others."

Earlier, analysts Jeffrey Christian, of New York-based CPM Group, and Rhona O'Connell, of London-based stockbroker T. Hoare & Co, argued European central banks do not hold enough gold in their reserves to make much difference, if sold, to the country economic ratios stipulated under the Maastricht Treaty as necessary for European monetary union.
-Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1641; email: clive.mckeef@reuters.com
